newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Canada rejects Anglo-US boycott of HK legislature.
newsitem.headline: Canada rejects Anglo-US boycott of HK legislature.

text.p: Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Monday he would attend the swearing-in of Hong Kong's new unelected legislature, refusing to join a British-American ministerial boycott.

Breaking ranks with fellow-Western allies, Axworthy said he would go to the inauguration of the controversial provisional legislature that China has appointed to replace an elected parliament after the colony's handover at midnight on Monday.
Britain opposes the dissolution of the present chamber, elected for four years in 1995 after democratic reforms were introduced in the twilight of London rule.

Axworthy told reporters he would attend the investiture although British Prime Minister Tony Blair, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright were staying away from the ceremony.
Axworthy's action added to a setback Britain has suffered over the past week as its ministerial boycott crumbled, with other countries shunning the action.
Even Britain and the United States gave a bow to reality last week as the boycott plan disintegrated by deciding to send along their top career diplomats to the swearing-in ceremony.
Axworthy said Canada had an important stake in Hong Kong, and intended to maintain a close relationship with the new Hong Kong administration led by Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa.
Canada has more than 30,000 citizens in Hong Kong, although the number may be far higher because many Hong Kong people who have emigrated to Canada are believed to have returned.

Asked if he would attend the swearing-in, he said he would, and added: "At the same time, we want to convey that Canada expects China to live up to its commitments regarding Hong Kong's autonomy, its institutions and way of life."
He said he had met Chief Secretary Anson Chan, the territory's top civil servant, on Monday and would meet Tung on Wednesday and Democratic Party head Martin Lee on Tuesday.
Britain's Prince Charles will formally hand Hong Kong back to Chinese President Jiang Zemin at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday, marking the end of more than 150 years of British rule.
